title: Personal Hygiene & Handwashing
blurb: How to wash your hands properly, keep yourself tidy for food work, and stay away from food when you are ill.
siteNotes: Where the hand wash basins, soap and paper towels are in each food area
Where blue plasters are kept and who issues them
The venue rule on jewellery, perfume and uniform for food areas
Who you tell if you are ill, and how (phone, text or in person)
legalNotes: Good personal hygiene and handwashing are core food hygiene practice: Food Safety Act 1990 and Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 on the hygiene of foodstuffs, Annex II chapter VIII (personal hygiene), as retained in law in England. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2004/852
CHECK: the 20 second wash time is common guidance rather than a figure in the regulation; confirm it matches the venue food safety management system.
CHECK: the 48 hours symptom-free rule matches Food Standards Agency guidance for vomiting and diarrhoea; confirm the venue policy says the same, and what applies to other illnesses.
Blue plasters, short nails, no varnish or false nails, hair covered and minimal jewellery are standard good practice in food areas. The trainer lists them; no figures are added.

cards.title: Personal Hygiene & Handwashing
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- wash your hands properly, and at the right times
- keep yourself tidy and covered in food areas
- report illness and stay away from food

cards.title: Hands touch everything
cards.body: Good personal hygiene is one of the most powerful ways we keep guests safe from illness, and handwashing is at the top of the list. Our hands can carry bacteria from a door handle or a raw ingredient straight onto a plate of food.

items.title: Door handle
items.text: Bacteria picked up on the way.

items.title: Raw ingredient
items.text: Carried on hands to other food.

items.title: Guest's plate
items.text: Where it can make someone ill.

cards.title: Soap, warm water, 20 seconds
cards.body: A quick rinse is not washing. Scrub all over, then dry your hands.

items.title: Scrub all over
items.text: Palms, backs, between fingers and thumbs.

cards.title: When to wash your hands
cards.body: Wash properly and often. These are the times you must not skip it.

items.title: After face or hair
items.text: Touching them puts bacteria on your hands.

items.title: New task
items.text: Wash before you start the next job.

cards.title: Keep yourself tidy
cards.body: Beyond hands, keep everything else in order. A blue plaster is easy to spot if it comes off into food.

left.title: Do
items: Cuts covered with a blue (detectable) plaster

right.title: Do not
items: Nail varnish or false nails in food areas
Strong perfume or aftershave around food
Loose hair in a food area
Cover a cut with any old plaster

cards.title: Report it and stay away from food
cards.body:
If you have vomiting or diarrhoea, you must report it and stay away from food. Be symptom-free for at least 48 hours before you handle food again.

> It can feel like letting the team down, but coming in could put dozens of guests at risk. If in doubt, speak to your manager.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Soap, warm water, at least 20 seconds, then dry
- Wash after the toilet, raw food or waste, face or hair, and new tasks
- Short clean nails, hair covered, cuts under a blue plaster
- Ill with vomiting or diarrhoea: report it and stay away from food until 48 hours symptom-free

cards.q: How long should you wash your hands for?
options: A few quick seconds under the tap
cards.why: Scrub all over for at least 20 seconds, then dry. A quick rinse is not enough.

cards.q: You should wash your hands after handling raw food.
cards.why: Hands can carry bacteria from raw food onto other food, so wash straight after.

cards.q: Cuts in a food area should be covered with…
options: Any plaster that is to hand
Nothing, if it is a small cut
cards.why: A blue plaster is easy to spot if it comes off, so it can be found before it reaches a guest.

cards.q: Nail varnish and false nails are fine in food-handling areas.
cards.why: Nails should be short and clean, with no varnish or false nails in food areas.

cards.q: After a sickness bug, how long should you be symptom-free before handling food?
cards.why: You must be symptom-free for at least 48 hours before you handle food again.

cards.q: Handwashing means soap and warm water, not just a quick rinse.
cards.why: Proper washing uses soap and warm water and scrubs all over.

cards.q: Name one time (other than after raw food) that you must wash your hands.
options: Only at the end of your shift
Only when your hands look dirty
After touching your face or hair
Once an hour, on the hour
cards.why: You wash after the toilet, after waste, after touching your face or hair, and when you start a new task.

cards.q: If you have vomiting or diarrhoea you should report it and stay away from food.
cards.why: Coming in ill could put dozens of guests at risk. Report it and speak to your manager.

cards.q: Hair in a food area should be…
cards.why: Hair should be tied back or covered in food areas.

cards.q: Why is good personal hygiene so important in our job?
options: It makes the venue look smarter
It is only needed for inspections
It stops bacteria reaching our guests
cards.why: Good hygiene protects guests from illness by keeping bacteria off food.
